DW1d0I5DksG.content:
We’ve been fighting housing discrimination for more than 𝟓𝟎 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬.

It’s a legacy we think about this month, in particular: 𝐀𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐥 𝐢𝐬 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐫 𝐇𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡.

It’s the month when the 1968 Fair Housing Act was signed, the month when the Civil Rights Act of 1866 – the first federal law to ban discrimination in housing – passed Congress.

𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲. 𝐕𝐢𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐭. 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝, 𝐭𝐨𝐨.

Every day, we receive reports from Virginians facing housing bias. Most involve disability discrimination. In recent months, we’ve heard about landlords who won’t provide accessible parking or refuse tenants their right to install a shower bar. These aren’t just cruel actions. They’re unlawful.

And they involve a disability nearly all of us, and all of our older friends and relatives, know well: the loss of mobility with age.

Every year of this work is a challenge. But we face new threats today. The Trump administration is defunding the enforcement of civil rights laws in housing and interfering with Virginia’s own fair housing protections.

Virginians are counting on us. That’s why we’re asking: 𝐏𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚 𝐅𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐇𝐎𝐌𝐄 𝐛𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. For as little as $10 a month, you can join the fight for housing justice.

Your support matters this month – and every month.

At Mayor Danny Avula’s first State of the City event last week in Southside, @homesforallourneighbors coalition members spoke about Code Refresh — and additional strategies the City and nonprofit partners can embrace to expand housing access and affordability.

Thomas Okuda Fitzpatrick, executive director of @homeofva, told the audience: "We're jazzed about the Code Refresh — if — if it ensures that there's equitable distribution of the way we use land." He explained that we need to create new housing not only in neighborhoods that have already faced development pressure, but citywide.

Jovan Burton, executive director of the Partnership for Housing Affordability, noted that recent population growth in Richmond has mostly come from households earning more than $150,000, further reducing the already too-small number of homes for lower- and middle-income residents.

Karen O’Brien, CEO of CARITAS, pointed to the need for housing across the lifecycle. She shared the bracing fact that older adults are “the fastest growing population of unhoused people.”

Learn more — and get involved with us: @homesforallourneighbors.

[Photos by Ross Catrow, City of Richmond]

#CodeRefresh #Richmond #FairHousing

📢 Big news from the General Assembly: a slate of tenant protection bills is moving forward in the Senate!

From expanding access to the courts, to limiting excessive attorney’s fees, to stabilizing mobile home parks, these bills are about one simple idea: 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗿 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲, 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Laura Dobbs, Director of Policy for @homeofva, made clear why we need bills like HB848, giving tenants a new way to seek justice: 

"Under current law, a tenant who falls behind on rent—often because their home is uninhabitable—is locked out of the courthouse while their landlord faces zero accountability."

And Kashish Pillai, Policy Analyst at @newvamajority warned about the risks to mobile home residents:

“As private equity firms increasingly acquire mobile home parks… the long-term stability and affordability of mobile home parks are under serious threat. At a time when affordability is top of mind for voters and legislators alike, manufactured home communities are one of the last pathways to truly affordable homeownership. These bills provide essential protections. ”

Together with @aha_virginia, we’re advocating for policies that 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱 — so tenants can hold landlords accountable for dangerous conditions, avoid unnecessary eviction, and stay rooted in their communities.

These bills aren’t radical. They’re fair. And they’re urgently needed.

Now they need full Senate approval. Stay tuned — and stay engaged!

Mia was working in a temporary job at the DMV when a short-term position at HOME opened in 1995. She recalls joining a “tight-knit team” in a two-story house on Richmond’s Cary Street. “I was one of the youngest employees when I started,” Mia told us during a recent staff meeting, “and now I think I’m one of the oldest!” She says she has stayed so long, serving a countless number of people working to buy their first homes, because “the work is a reward in itself.”

But Mia has weathered storms. The 2008 financial crisis spread foreclosures like wildfire and sapped opportunities for first-time buyers to secure their first homes. She supported clients through the inflated pandemic-era market, when successful buyers often had to bid above listing prices and were asked to waive inspections. Now she confronts new headwinds amid high interest rates and the threat of reduced federal support for homeownership.

Through it all, she has been grateful to “build a special bond with clients.” And today, she finds her connections with some first-time buyers to be like that of a mom or older sister—with all the confidence and clarity experience can bring. She also appreciates the flexibility HOME has offered; she was able to bring her daughter to work a few months after giving birth, and continues to make time for family that now includes two daughters and a granddaughter.

“I can’t imagine life after HOME,” Mia says. “There’s no place like it.”

"UNDERLYING THE NEW URBANIST VISION of community is a critique of suburban sprawl . . . which focuses on the pernicious effects of single-use development, resulting in segregation by age, income, and function. Absent a regional plan, suburban land is developed in restricted functions and uses: dwellings of a certain type and cost in one area, shopping malls in another area, industrial parks in another area with the consequent absence of a coherent sense of place and community and a life revolving instead around the automobile and clogged express- ways. As Andres Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk-the two leading New Urbanists-wrote in 1992, the proliferation of isolated "planned communities' has resulted in a radical disjunction between the happy private space of the suburban homeowner and the extreme degradation of the public realm, with "traffic, commuting time, and the great distances from shopping, work, and entertainment" all cause for complaint. "The classic suburb is less a community than an agglomeration of houses shops, and offices connected to one another by cars, not by the fabric of human life. The structure of the suburb tends to confine people to their houses and cars; it discourages strolling, walking, mingling with neighbors. The suburb is the last word in privatization, perhaps even its lethal consum- mation, and it spells the end of authentic civic life." . . . 
 The New Urbanism is not, then, so much a break with the guiding tenets of earlier new town planning as it is a critique of the inadvertent results of that movement, whose integrated vision and idealism became caricatured in the hands of suburban developers, who first planted residential tracts without any town centers, then separate malls, and finally separate industrial parks."

Why does zoning reform inspire so much pushback? The allure of low-density is the false promise that it preserves a way of life. And fear of property value change. And... the "not in my backyard" myopia. But what's the cost?  Wise words:

"Rouse was also developing his ideas at a time when, following Levitt's example, suburbia was rapidly changing from farmland to tract housing. Rouse had a clear analysis of the factors that led inexorably to sprawl- chief among them the low-density residential zoning that communities imposed on development, in the belief that low density would preserve their way of life. C-bGzeYv59a.content:
Good example of housing options that help with the shortage - this tucked away little house on the left is on the property of the larger house, but is a separate dwelling. 

When you hear "single family zoning," it's important to also hear, "Mother-in-law suites should be illegal," which is a hard argument to make. Is it ethical to zone in such a way that a family cannot rent to a relative in need? 

Or  when a couple or individual no longer needs as large of a space, they can live in their ADU/suite and lease out their home for a good source of income later in life. 

ADUs, duplexes, etc. solve lots of problems in cities - and actually this is a good way to avoid having all the rural land and suburbs developed in every square inch. Let cities be more dense, and the countryside is preserved.

C9lu3ZeNuOu.content:
Walkability and zoning reform go hand in hand, and make for beautiful and welcoming places!

A few pictures:
1) Local campaign to end single-family zoning in the city 
2) A snapshot of how mixed use zoning makes places where you really love to live!
3) Example 1 of what ending single family zoning allows: the mother-in-law suite or ADU
4) Example 2: the cottage court, or groups of starter home for affordable housing to address the "missing middle" problem 

There are very understandable reasons that some are concerned about zoning reform, and I do empathize. To affirm greater freedom for land use does carry some risk. 

Organizations like StrongTowns offers much to address these risks! 

Yet exclusionary zoning policies such as single-family-only rules also carry real risks for cities. Should policies that were created for racial, class, and income segregation be maintained? Can we effectively welcome, as a city, with these policies in place? 

Can we have zoning that allows a city to value young professionals, refugees, the elderly, and others not interested, licensed, or able to drive cars? Will they find walkable spaces to live and belong in this community? Allowing some density means allowing walkability. 

Most places in Southwest VA will not be like this, but our cities have the opportunity to be the kinds of places people love to visit, and even more, the kinds of places people love to live.

Any effort to curb pedestrian deaths and accident fatalities involves slowing cars down in areas that have multiple access points.

When people see areas where these projects have been done, i.e., the aftermath, they almost always love them - the locations become good places for people and not just cars. The outcomes are popular and good for business.
